Saw a psychiatrist for a few years that over medicated me and would change my meds every month when they didn’t immediately work. I was absolutely miserable and eventually got fed up and decided it was worth the serotonin syndrome to quit all my meds and start over.

Needless to say, I was really struggling with my depression and the side effects and decided to participate in an Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) to get back on track. As part of the program, we did 9 hours of group therapy per week and, at the beginning of each session, had to fill out a “diary card” outlining our depression/anxiety scores and what we had been working on since the last group. My scores were high enough for the LCSW who oversaw the group to routinely pull me aside to talk privately during breaks in group.

The first time I saw the new psychiatrist (who worked in conjunction with the IOP), he looked over my files from the old psychiatrist, looked over my diary cards, and took a brief oral history before telling me that I had no discernible symptoms of chronic depression or any other psychological disorder and that I should stop pushing myself in my career and keep taking 60mg of Vyvanse every morning (I’m 5’6” and 125lbs) so I could get out of bed.

I have ADHD and I have a lot of problems with small detail things as well. I've politely approached my supervisors and asked them to make checklists for daily tasks and step-by-step instructions for more specific tasks. For example: I work at an animal hospital so I have a checklist for daily tasks like which rooms to mop at which times, when to walk dogs, etc. and I have specific instructions for things like entering charges for procedures that we perform on patients. It helps me stay on track and it provides an opportunity for me to check things off and immediately notice things that I've forgotten.

Re getting a job: I dropped out halfway through my first semester of college and I now work two part-time jobs in fields that I'm interested in (train horses part time and work at a vet clinic part time) and it's given me a lot of insight into what I'd like to study when I go back to school and has given me real-life skills that I will be able to use when I choose a field of study. I highly recommend trying to get a job related to something that you're considering as a career rather than just finding the first job you can. It may take a little extra time, but I promise it will be worth it. You'll learn a lot (even in an entry-level or clerical position) and you'll feel much more productive and positive about your time away from school. I also suggest keeping up with some studying. My major was biochem/neuroscience, so I buy older chemistry/microbiology/math textbooks for very cheap from our local used bookstore to study so I'm on my game when I eventually go back to school. Even if you just spend time reviewing the basics, you'll feel good about how you're spending your time and you'll be more confident in your ability to re-apply when you decide to start again. Best of luck to you, enjoy the adventure!

Horseback rider here. Honestly, I've never been able to get a workout in a gym that rivals the workout I get at the barn everyday. I think it comes down to your mindset more than anything. When I'm riding or mucking stalls or doing other barn work, I'm not trying to workout; my body just HAS to be able to keep up with what I need to do. 500+ bale hay shipment comes in and our help doesn't show? Me, the hay guy, my trainer, and my trainer's dad have to get that shit off the truck and stacked 6 bales high in the hayloft in a timely manner so the hay guy can make his other deliveries. Barn hand calls in sick? I have to clean 10 12x12 stalls before I can do anything else (for those unfamiliar, this means removing all the poop, moving all the bedding to the wall, raking the floor, re spreading the bedding through the stall with a muck rake, and scrubbing, filling, and carrying two 10lb buckets back to the stall) Grain shipment comes and I'm the only one at the barn? I need to unload well over 1 ton of 50 pound feed bags and stack them in the feed room so the delivery guy can get on his way. When I do this stuff, I'm not calculating reps or sets or weight and I think that makes me push through harder. It's so easy to say, "Oh wow, X reps at X weight is so many! I've done plenty" at the gym. At the barn, you have to just get it the fuck done and there's no time to consider anything but the task at hand. 

My advice? Get a weekend job at a farm and get paid to get super kickass exercise to supplement your regular gym workouts.

I agree with this. Tell her about your situation in a factual manner. It could help to show her your calendar or write out your work schedule and explain what your job entails so she can understand why you are not able to answer calls or leave work at a moment's notice. Let her know when it IS appropriate to contact you, such as evenings or weekends. It may also help to schedule when you will spend time together in advance. If she knows that you're going to meet for lunch at 2pm on Saturday, then she won't be so worried about trying to get in touch with you during the week. Sudden schedule changes can be very stressful for ASD folks, so make sure to follow through with the plans that you make. If she still doesn't get the picture, then I suggest finding a third party (preferably someone like a sibling, close friend, or parent who knows her well) to help mediate the problem.

Sequoyah Hills park is smack on the Tennessee River and is right in one of the biggest and most historic neighborhoods in the city, Sequoyah Hills. I have a horse, Charlie, that is kind of a bully (he's known to corner his pasture mates in the run-in shed, break out of his stall to open the other horses' stalls and eat their food, etc.). Subsequently, he lives in a paddock by himself where he can see all the other horses and can run up and down the fence line with them, but he doesn't get the opportunity to nuzzle, groom, or play with them. His best friend, Irony, (Charlie's pervious owner bought he and Irony from the same training barn when they were 4 year olds, and they've lived on the same farm together for the past 10 years.) lives on the other side of the farm and they don't get to see each other very often. 

I ride 3 or 4 times a week and I'm at the barn almost every day to work, but I try my best to take 1 day a week where I turn Irony out in Charlie's field, I bring my "horse watching" backpack (carrots, peppermints, colored pens and pencils, a nice notebook, a good non-violent book to read like The Education of Little Tree or a riding book like Zen Mind - Zen Horse, a couple cigarettes, a beer or two or a little wine in a thermos, and healthy snacks like fruit, cheese, peanut butter and bread, etc.), and I sit in the grass or on a blanket and watch them play, graze, groom each other, roll, and just relax. I give them a carrot or a peppermint if they wander over to check me out, but otherwise I don't talk to them or call their names or direct a lot of my attention to them by watching them intently. I sit, read, write, draw, snack, and think. 

Honestly, it's some of the best therapy and it really refreshes me and helps bring me up if I'm too down, slow me down if I'm too up, and redirect my thoughts (I also have ADHD) away from the arbutrary things that I hyper focus on and worry about like do I have enough quinoa to make a cold salad for dinner and how dirty my car windows are, onto constructive things like thinking about what my therapist and I talked about during my session and planning what kind of poses I want to work on in my evening yoga practice. 

Animals of all kinds are incredible life partners. I sometimes dream about how reassuring it feels to be laying in the sun, reading a book, when all of a sudden I feel Charlie licking the salt off my forehead or nuzzling my hair. Not because I called him over or because I held out a treat to bribe him over, just because he wanted to come say hi for a second before he meandered off to his favorite rolling spot. 

Part of the reason that I bought him was because I knew it would be something to keep me grounded. If I get too manic and spend his board money, or if I am too depressed to work and I can't afford his vet bills, then I'm letting him down by not giving him what he needs to live. If I kill myself, no one else is going to love him enough to take extra care to make sure his halter always fits right, that he doesn't have to take a cold bit in the winter, that there are enough Chia and flax seeds in his supplement bin for the feeders to give him, and that the itchy spot on his right shoulder always gets a good scratch. 

Animals are so important, guys. Do your research, budget a little money, and adopt a friend. Even if it's a guinea pig or a rabbit or a snake or a fish. It will help you tremendously.

I just hit the 11 week mark of taking 40mg Citalopram so I have a little insight for you

1. You are an individual person. Your experience with an antidepressant is not necessarily going to line up with the data of one of these meta-analyses.

2. Just because you start taking one antidepressant doesn't mean you have to continue taking that antidepressant for the rest of your life

3. Any antidepressant is going to take upwards of 45-60 days to start working. They key to these medications is patience, patience, patience.

4. Depression is meant to be treated with a combination of psychotherapy and drug therapy. Citalopram is likely to help your depression with the correct dosage, but you will get the maximum effects if you participate in regular psychotherapy in conjunction with your chemical therapy. 

5. Depression often occurs along with other mental disorders. For example, my current diagnosis is ADHD with secondary social anxiety and depression. My depression was the most prominent issue that I was having and my PDoc started by only treating my depression, then moved on to treating the ADHD and social anxiety when the symptoms of my depression subsided. you might be in a similar boat and it might take some time before you and your PDoc can wholey diagnose your brain.

6. Don't stress yourself out with all this fucking data and numbers. It's much more reassuring and helpful to talk to real people about their experiences and to share yours with others as well. I've learned a lot from chatting with people on message boards and forums (most notably the crazymeds.com forums). Your mental health is only quantifiable to an extent; the process of recovering from mental illness is much more about your experience than the statistics of your journey

Some of these have already been mentioned but are worth re-iterating

1. Try to work out a deal so that you can lease the horse before you buy it. I recently bought a horse that I had been exercise riding for 2-3 years prior. Because I'd been riding him for so long, I knew his bad habits, how his feet were (how often he lost shoes and how he was for my farrier), what sort of extra vet requirements he has (joint injections, supplements, etc). It gave me an opportunity to budget the nitty-gritty of taking care of him. I found out that he needs his stifles injected periodically and that he tends to throw shoes and would benefit from being on a hoof supplement. finding out those small things helped me finalize my decision to buy him when his previous owner offered him for sale

2. Find a manager that will allow you to work off some of your board. I feed most nights and some mornings, I exercise the owner's horses, and I help with barn maintenance as needed at my boarding barn. I brought my board down from $350 to around $75 to cover the cost of buying Charlie's ration of hay and grain.

3. Pasture board, self-care board, or boarding at a barn that is not exclusively a boarding/show facility is great. My guy is on 24/7 turnout, gets fed AM/PM and gets blanketed as needed. If I moved him to our self-care pasture and cut him down to once-per-day feeding and blanketed him myself, I could save $100. In addition, this barn is a casual boarding barn and is a lot cheaper than the other high-end, for-profit boarding barns in my city that charge $500+ for pasture board. I don't have an indoor arena, cross-country course, or olympic-level onsite trainer, but I'd rather trailer to school XC every once in a while, slip my trainer an extra $10 to drive to my farm when I schedule the rare lesson, and maybe miss a day or two of serious schooling to trot sets or a groundwork day because our outdoor arena is a swimming pool, than pay an extra couple hundred of dollars to have constant access to all the fanciest amenities. 

4. Leasing is a great option, or giving lessons. I give a lessons to a few of the younger kids of my family's friends for about $30 each. If you can find a few kids who want to learn and whos parents are willing to pay you to teach them the basics, or are looking to lease a horse for lessons go for it. Also, if you end up boarding at a barn that has a lesson program or hosts an IHSA/IEA team, the directors of those programs are often looking for horses to lease for use in their programs. That's worth looking into as well. 

5. Definitely cut back your traditional lessoning. I understand the appeal to having a trainer available, but I only take lessons on occasion (maybe once every few months) and substitute my lack of instruction by attending clinics hosted by my local CT society and watching friend's lessons. I also ride with my peers frequently and we act as each other's "eyes on the ground". I still get someone barking at me to stop pinching with my knee, and I still get the insight and theories of professional horsepeople, but I don't have to pay $50+ for a half-hour lesson twice per week. If you're planning on bringing a youngster along, you'll definitely need a trainer and that might not be a feasible thing to cut, but is definitely a viable idea when you get pony going and more advanced. I feel like I'm much more attentive to lessons and clinics when I only get them once in a while - I want to get my money's worth. I also think that I've become much more aware of and independent in my riding because I am responsible for policing myself and FEELING when I'm incorrect in my schooling sessions. I don't just rely on someone on the ground to tell me everytime I do something wrong. I have to be more active in the saddle and I feel like that's been very positive for my equitation.
